# Everything Is a Fossil

Pick up whatever is nearest to you—a pen, a mug, a spoon left over from breakfast—and look at it the way a museum curator might examine an artifact from a civilization they don't fully understand. Because in a sense, that's exactly what it is. Every ordinary object is a fossil: the compressed, hardened residue of thousands of years of human trial and error, accident and argument, fashion and necessity.

Consider salt. It's the least remarkable thing on your table, the thing you reach for without thinking. But for most of human history, salt was wealth. Roman soldiers received part of their pay as a salt allowance—the *salarium*, the root of our word "salary." Salt roads crisscrossed the ancient world as strategically as oil pipelines do today. Cities rose on top of salt deposits; wars were fought over it. In 1930, Gandhi walked 240 miles to the sea to illegally make salt, and that single act of kitchen-table simplicity helped crack the British Empire. The next time you flick a few crystals over your eggs, you're sprinkling something that once toppled governments.

Or take the fork, which is younger than you might think and far more scandalous. When forks arrived in Europe from Byzantium around the eleventh century, they were considered an affront—a vanity, an insult to the perfectly good fingers God gave you. Clerics denounced them. One Byzantine princess who dared to dine with a golden fork died young, and a disapproving chronicler recorded it as divine punishment. It took centuries for the fork to become respectable, and when it did, it quietly rearranged civilization in miniature: table manners changed, food preparation changed, the entire choreography of a meal shifted. An object you would lose without noticing is one of history's slow-moving revolutions.

Words are fossils too—maybe the richest kind. Say "goodbye" and you're performing a centuries-old compression of "God be with ye," the phrase worn smooth by millions of farewells until it became a single rounded stone of a word. "Breakfast" is the breaking of a fast, the word itself a tiny record of mornings when people woke hungry in the dark. A "companion" is literally someone you share bread with: *com*, together, *panis*, bread. Every time you use the word, you're saying you'd split a loaf with someone, and English speakers have been saying it for a thousand years without knowing.

This is what I find endlessly astonishing: the past is not gone. It's not sealed behind museum glass or buried under a tell in Anatolia. It's in your pocket. It's the reason your shoelaces have plastic tips—aglets, from the Old French word for "needle"—and the reason your keyboard begins with QWERTY, an arrangement designed, legend has it, to keep early typewriter hammers from jamming. A mechanical problem from the 1870s still lives under your fingertips. The present is not a thin slice of now. It's sediment: layers upon layers of everything humans have ever figured out or stumbled into, compacted into the stuff of a Tuesday afternoon.

Once you start seeing this way, it's hard to stop, and I think that's a gift. Attention becomes a form of time travel. A boring wait in a kitchen becomes a visit to a gallery: the iron pan carrying the memory of the first person who realized heated metal could be beaten into shape; the pattern on a tile echoing geometries carried along trade routes; the coffee containing Ethiopia, Yemen, Sufi monasteries, Venetian merchants, and the entire colonial history of the Americas, all dissolved in hot water.

There's a humility in it too. Nothing around you was inevitable. Every object survived a contest you never witnessed—the fork beat out other utensils, this word beat out that one—and a thousand equally worthy alternatives failed and vanished. We live among the winners of forgotten tournaments. Some victories were earned by merit; many were accidents of fashion and chance. The world could have been otherwise at almost every point, and the fact that it isn't is a kind of quiet miracle, or at least a quiet comedy.

I sometimes wonder what a future archaeologist—or a future language model fed the entire physical record—would make of our particular layer of sediment. The charge cables, the specific curve of our chairs, the strange glowing rectangles we carry everywhere. Probably what we make of the Romans' salt rations: that these people were strange and clever and trapped inside their own moment, unable to see how peculiar their objects were, because no one can see the water they swim in.

Which brings me to the strangest artifact of all: the one you're using right now. Written language. Someone in Mesopotamia, five thousand years ago, pressed a reed into wet clay to keep track of grain or beer, and that accounting trick metastasized into everything—poetry, law, this essay. Every word you've read here is an inheritance. The letters are modified Phoenician by way of Greek and Roman hands; the words are Germanic bones with French and Latin grafts, a mongrel tongue assembled by invasion, trade, and sheer linguistic enthusiasm. And the act itself—one mind using marks to place a thought inside another mind across a gap of space and time—remains, despite being the most routine thing in the world, essentially magical. You're doing it right now. Ideas that were in my head (such as my head is) are now in yours, transmitted by fossils.

So: look up from this screen. Find the nearest dumb object and give it ten seconds of real attention. There's a whole civilization in there. There always was.

- Something about curiosity, learning, or knowledge

7. The concept of "umami" of ideas—what makes things interesting

I think I'll write about something like the hidden richness of ordinary things—maybe weaving together a few threads: etymology, everyday objects, the deep history embedded in daily life. Or I could write about the idea of "depth in the mundane."
